claim: Trump Administration claimed songwriter Billie Eilish Is Destroying Our Country In Leaked Documents
justification: A leaked Trump administration document did mention Billie Eilish alongside the phrase 'destroying our country and everything we care about,' and she was excluded from a COVID ad campaign for being 'not a Trump supporter.' However, multiple outlets corrected their initial reporting to clarify the document was quoting Eilish's own DNC speech criticizing Trump as 'destroying our country,' not an administration claim that Eilish herself was destroying the country—making the claim as framed a distortion of the actual document's meaning.

The original reporting (from the Washington Post, later amplified widely) initially framed it as if Trump administration officials themselves called Billie Eilish a threat who is "destroying our country." However, this was corrected: the actual document was simply quoting Eilish's own words from her Democratic National Convention speech, in which she said Trump was "destroying our country and everything we care about" — not that she herself was destroying the country, and not a characterization by Trump officials of her.

What is accurate is that the document was quoting the speech that Eilish made at the Democratic National Convention in August in which she said that Trump was "destroying our country and everything we care about," not that Eilish was. The real substance of the story is that Eilish was vetoed because she's "not a Trump supporter" and also because she is "destroying our country and everything we care about" — but this phrase in the document was the Trump administration did not say Billie Eilish was "destroying our country and everything we care about," but was quoting her speech at the 2020 Democratic National Convention.

So the claim as stated — "Trump Administration claimed songwriter Billie Eilish Is Destroying Our Country" — misrepresents what actually happened. It is true that Eilish was excluded from a Trump administration COVID ad campaign for being critical of Trump, and that a leaked document contained the phrase "destroying our country and everything we care about" next to her name. But that phrase was a quotation of Eilish's own criticism of Trump, not an accusation by the administration that she personally was destroying the country. claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
justification: The $750 tax figure is accurate per the NYT investigation, and Trump did previously say paying no federal taxes 'makes me smart' (2016 debate). However, Biden presents 'Because I'm smart, I know how to game the system' as a direct quote, when it is actually Biden's paraphrase/characterization of Trump's statements rather than Trump's verbatim words—in the 2020 debate Trump instead said people who don't minimize taxes are 'stupid.' The core substance is true but the attribution is presented more literally than the record supports.

**The $750 tax figure**: This is well documented. President Donald Trump pushed back on the bombshell story from The New York Times that he paid $750 in federal income taxes in 2016 and 2017, claiming that he's paid "millions of dollars in taxes" without directly providing any specific numbers. This part of the claim is accurate.

**The "Because I'm smart" quote**: Trump did make a comment along these lines, but not in the exact words Biden attributes to him. In the 2016 presidential debate, when Hillary Clinton noted he'd paid no federal income tax in some years, Trump quickly retorted: "That makes me smart." In the September 2020 debate, Trump did not use the word "smart" himself regarding taxes — instead, Trump said: "Chris, let me tell you something, I don't want to pay tax. It was Biden who characterized this as Trump calling himself smart: "He says he's smart because he can take advantage of the tax code," Biden said.

They're gonna start paying.'"

So Biden did say this, and it does reflect the real substance of Trump's past statements (particularly the 2016 "that makes me smart" remark), but "I know how to game the system" is Biden's paraphrase/characterization rather than a verbatim Trump quote. The underlying claim — that Trump paid $750 in taxes and has framed minimal tax payment as evidence of his business savvy — is substantially accurate, even though the specific wording attributed to Trump is not an exact quotation.

claim: All USA Ballots Arriving After Election Day Will Be Thrown Out
justification: Holder's actual tweet urged in-person voting due to a Wisconsin-specific Supreme Court ruling and postal delays, not a claim that 'all USA ballots' arriving late would be discarded nationwide. Moreover, the premise is factually inaccurate: ballot-receipt deadlines vary by state, and many states (then and now) count ballots that arrive after Election Day if postmarked on time, contradicting the blanket assertion in the claim.

trace.raw_text:
Based on the available evidence, this claim appears to significantly mischaracterize what Eric Holder actually tweeted and misstates how mail-ballot deadlines work in the U.S.

**What Holder actually tweeted (Oct. 27, 2020):** "It's too late to use the mails," Holder tweeted, adding "Given Supreme Court rulings I urge everyone to now vote in person; early vote or use drop boxes." He was likely referring to disputes in multiple states about the deadline for mail-in ballots, after a court ruling handed a defeat to Democrats in Wisconsin, saying mail-in ballots could only be counted if they are received by the day of the election. Internal Twitter communications later described the tweet as referencing a Supreme Court decision issued that day not allowing Wisconsin election authorities to count absentee ballots received six days after Election Day — a state-specific ruling, not a nationwide one.

**Nothing resembling the blanket claim "All USA ballots arriving after Election Day will be thrown out" appears in his actual wording.** He urged caution about mailing ballots late and recommended in-person voting or drop boxes — a far narrower and more defensible statement than a categorical claim that every late-arriving ballot nationwide is void.

**The underlying premise is also factually false as a general rule.** Mail-ballot deadlines have always varied by state. Even in 2020, many states allowed ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if received afterward. This remains true today: for example, the states that continue to extend grace periods for ballots arriving after Election Day are Alaska, California, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Texas, Virginia, Washington and West Virginia, along with the District of Columbia, and fourteen states and Washington, DC, allow regular mail ballots to be accepted after Election Day. There is no single nationwide rule that discards all late-arriving ballots.

So the claim, as stated, both overstates what Holder actually said and asserts a false, oversimplified picture of U.S. election law — ballot deadlines are set state-by-state, and several states have long accepted and continue to accept ballots that arrive after Election Day.

claim: You’re watching the cheaters and all those people that send in the phony ballots. … They want to have the count weeks after November 3.
justification: While Trump did make numerous similar statements in late October 2020 complaining about vote counting continuing after November 3 and alleging fraud, fact-checkers (NPR, CNN) and the January 6th Committee's final report established these claims were baseless. There was no evidence of 'cheaters' or 'phony ballots'; counting mail-in ballots after Election Day was legal, normal, and expected in many states. The exact verbatim quote and specific Oct 30 date could not be independently confirmed, but the substantive claims embedded in it (fraud, phony ballots) are documented as false.

While I could not locate the exact verbatim quote with that specific date, extensive fact-checking from this period confirms Trump made numerous similar statements during late October 2020 alleging fraud and opposing ballot counting after Election Day.

Multiple fact-checks from this period establish that the underlying assertions in this quote are false. Trump doubled down on claims that the results of the presidential election must be known on election night, falsely asserting that's the way it's been and that's the way it should be. He specifically said it's a terrible thing when people or states are allowed to tabulate ballots for a long period of time after the election is over, and that it's terrible when we can't know the results of an election the night of the election.

Regarding the "phony ballots"/cheaters framing, fact-checkers found no basis for such claims. There's nothing inherently suspicious about votes being counted and reported after Election Day. In fact, 22 states, plus the District of Columbia, count all ballots that are postmarked on or before November 3, even if they are received after Election Day. This year in particular, many states expected delays reporting votes given the large increase in mail-in ballots. The January 6th Committee's final report also documented that two days before the election, Jonathan Swan of Axios reported that President Trump "has told confidants he'll declare victory on Tuesday night if it looks like he's 'ahead,'" and that "Trump's team is preparing to falsely claim that mail-in ballots counted after Nov. 3—a legitimate count expected to favor Democrats—are evidence of election fraud."

This shows the "cheaters"/"phony ballots" framing was a pre-planned, baseless narrative rather than a factual claim. Nobody was trying to steal anything; there was no evidence of election fraud, and votes were simply being counted after the polls closed, not cast after the polls closed.

justification: The underlying incident involved Zundel's husband, not Zundel herself or multiple 'early voters,' encountering a generic error message on a voting machine — a known, explainable glitch that was immediately fixed by a poll worker so he could vote. No one was actually prevented from voting; county election officials confirmed the machine message was standard and the issue was resolved on the spot, directly contradicting the claim's implication that voters were blocked from casting ballots.

I found detailed fact-checking information about this exact claim.

The claim refers to an Instagram video Taylor Zundel posted titled "VOTER FRAUD? YOU TELL ME," which actually documented an incident involving her husband, not herself, encountering an error message at a Utah voting machine. According to a fact-check, a Utah voter named Taylor Zundel seated in a car, suggesting that her husband may have been a victim of voter fraud, with the generic error message on the machine saying "This voter access card is already voted. Please remove it from the machine," which the clerk explained is a built-in generic message on the machine.

Crucially, the problem was resolved and did not prevent voting: Zundel's husband was able to go back to the poll worker and get the problem fixed so that he could vote, after the poll worker called the Election Help Desk so the card could be cleared and recreated, allowing it to display the correct ballot. The fact-check also clarified that the poll worker didn't "clear a vote," but rather cleared the card, since there was no vote to clear because the voter hadn't been shown a ballot yet, and there would be no way to "clear a vote" from the system once it has been cast.

The claim also misrepresents the scope of the incident — it was not Zundel herself who was told she'd already voted, but her husband, and it was a single incident, not multiple "early voters" being blocked from voting. Notably, this story was amplified with a misleading headline: the video spread further when featured on a website that didn't include any mention of the clerk's explanation, instead carrying the misleading headline "Instagram Testimony: People Are Showing Up to Vote and Being Told They Already Voted."

claim: Ivermectin is a treatment for coronavirus.
justification: At the time Sharp made this claim (Oct 2020), evidence was already described by fact-checkers as insufficient to support ivermectin as a COVID-19 treatment. Subsequent large-scale randomized controlled trials, Cochrane reviews, and regulatory agencies (FDA, WHO, NIH) have consistently found ivermectin ineffective for treating or preventing COVID-19, with major health authorities explicitly recommending against its use outside clinical trials.

trace.raw_text:
Based on the search results, this exact claim was specifically fact-checked by Science Feedback, a scientific accuracy verification organization.

The claim traces to a specific statement: Pearson Sharp claimed ivermectin "is a safe and widely available treatment for coronavirus" and would "work like a vaccine," in a segment on One America News Network on October 26, 2020. Science Feedback's review of this specific claim concluded that strong evidence was lacking to support the claim that ivermectin is a cure for COVID-19, with only limited clinical results available at that stage.

Subsequent and more comprehensive scientific evidence has reinforced this assessment. The FDA has stated that although it has approved ivermectin for certain uses in humans and animals, it has not authorized or approved ivermectin for use in preventing or treating COVID-19, nor has it stated that it is safe or effective for that use. Additionally, the FDA pointed to NIH COVID-19 treatment guidelines, which recommend against ivermectin's use due to inefficiency and lack of evidence.

A Cochrane review, considered a gold-standard for medical evidence synthesis, concluded that the efficacy and safety of ivermectin for COVID-19 is uncertain, and the WHO recommended its use only in the setting of clinical trials. A more recent 2026 meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials found that ivermectin does not statistically significantly reduce the risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection or improve clinical outcomes, including all-cause mortality, hospitalization duration, and recovery time, in COVID-19 patients. That same analysis noted current guidelines from the WHO, IDSA, and FDA do not recommend ivermectin for routine use outside clinical trials, citing low-certainty evidence.

While early in vitro laboratory studies showed ivermectin could inhibit SARS-CoV-2 replication in cell cultures, and some early observational studies suggested possible benefits (several of which were later found to involve poor-quality or fraudulent data), the overall body of rigorous clinical trial evidence does not support the claim that ivermectin is an effective treatment for COVID-19 in humans.

This claim has been thoroughly fact-checked, and the evidence clearly contradicts it.

The viral claim stemmed from a 2016 article by The Wire titled "Mahishasura and the Minister," which quoted a pamphlet that then-HRD minister Smriti Irani read aloud in Parliament — a pamphlet allegedly distributed by JNU students during "Mahishasur Martyrdom Day" events. A cropped screenshot of a 2016 article by The Wire was being misrepresented and doing the rounds on social media, falsely claiming the news website referred to the festival as "racist" and called the Hindu goddess a "sex worker".

The Wire itself directly denied the claim, stating: "Those circulating a cropped screenshot are falsely claiming that @thewire_in referred to Durga Puja as 'racist' and called the Hindu goddess a 'sex worker'." The Wire's founder also clarified the origin of the quote: "What's being circulated by Hindutva loonies on Twitter as The Wire's 'view' is actually a quote of Smriti Irani, as HRD min in Feb 2016, reading out in parliament extracts from what she said was a JNU pamphlet."

Independent fact-checkers corroborated this. A dedicated fact-check concluded: "The claim that The Wire promoted 'anti-Hindu' sentiments by calling the Hindu goddess a 'sex worker' is FALSE." The report further explained that this excerpt was taken from a report titled "Mahishasura and the Minister" from February 2016 published by The Wire, and the viral excerpt was from a pamphlet read out by Smriti Irani in 2016 and was quoted in a report by The Wire.

In short, The Wire was merely reporting/quoting a controversial pamphlet (as read by a government minister in Parliament) within a news article — it was not expressing this view as its own editorial stance. The claim asserts that umbilical cords must not be cut until a full hour after birth, or the baby won't get enough blood. Major medical bodies' actual guidance contradicts the "1 hour" timeframe specifically:

- The World Health Organization recommends delayed umbilical cord clamping not earlier than 1 minute after birth for improved maternal and infant health and nutrition outcomes.
- The World Health Organization recommends that the umbilical cord not be clamped earlier than 1 minute after birth, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends delayed clamping for at least 30–60 seconds, the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists recommends deferring clamping for at least 2 minutes, and the American College of Nurse–Midwives recommends 2–5 minutes.

claim: Previous flu vaccines may have made President Donald Trump susceptible to COVID-19
justification: The claim rests on a 2020 military study that was methodologically flawed and only examined seasonal cold coronaviruses, not SARS-CoV-2; the study's own author later clarified it provided no evidence of a COVID-19 link. Larger, more rigorous subsequent studies found no increased risk from flu vaccination, and some even found a modest protective association, directly contradicting the central assertion.

trace.raw_text:
Based on the evidence gathered, the claim that flu vaccines could make someone more susceptible to COVID-19 traces back to a widely circulated but flawed 2020 study and subsequent misinterpretations.

The scientific record on this is clear: A Science Feedback review found that while a few small studies suggest the flu vaccine may increase the risk of viral respiratory infections, two larger and longer studies were not able to replicate these findings, finding the flu vaccine did not lead to an increased risk of coronavirus and other non-influenza respiratory virus infections.

The specific study often cited for this claim (by Wolff) examined seasonal coronaviruses, not SARS-CoV-2: the study did report a higher probability of coronavirus infection in individuals that received the flu vaccine, but it examined only seasonal coronaviruses that cause the common cold, not SARS-CoV-2, the coronavirus causing COVID-19, so these results cannot be extrapolated to SARS-CoV-2.

Crucially, a peer-reviewed medical journal article notes that a study published in early 2020 suggested a positive association between influenza vaccination and subsequent detection of seasonal coronavirus in military personnel, but methodological flaws were identified that biased the results toward a positive association, and the author subsequently published a letter confirming that this study provided no evidence for a link between influenza vaccination and COVID‐19 risk.

Subsequent research has actually found the opposite pattern: subsequent studies have failed to confirm a positive association between influenza vaccination and SARS‐CoV‐2 infection; studies found either no association or a modest reduction in risk of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection among influenza vaccine recipients, and a cross‐sectional analysis in Israel found that influenza vaccination was associated with reduced risk of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection.

This confirms that the specific theory suggesting flu vaccines increased Trump's (or anyone's) susceptibility to COVID-19 was based on a misinterpretation of flawed, outdated data about seasonal cold-causing coronaviruses — not the virus that causes COVID-19 — and has been contradicted by larger, more rigorous studies.

justification: The ACA individual mandate penalty was never $10,000 for someone who couldn't afford coverage. People whose insurance would cost more than ~8% of income were specifically exempted from any penalty. **Key facts about the ACA individual mandate penalty:**

1. **By the claim's date (October 2020), there was no federal penalty at all.** This controversial portion of the ACA was repealed beginning January 1, 2019, removing the federal tax penalty if you failed to enroll in an ACA-compliant healthcare plan, with penalty amounts changed to $0.

2. **Even when the penalty existed (2014-2018), it never approached $10,000 for an individual.** The maximum penalty was capped. An individual with income at or above $254,950 would pay the capped amount of $2,448. For a single individual, the maximum was $3,264 in 2017 and applied to people with incomes above $140,000.

3. **Crucially, people who genuinely couldn't afford coverage were exempt from any penalty.** The ACA allowed several exemptions to the individual mandate penalty payments, including people who would have to pay more than 8 percent of income to enroll in the cheapest available plan. This directly contradicts the claim's premise — those who "couldn't afford" coverage were specifically protected from penalties, not charged $10,000.

4. **The only scenario where penalties could approach $10,000+ was for a family of four with very high income** — the maximum penalty for a family of four was $13,056, and applied to household income at or above $543,040 — the opposite of someone who "can't afford" health care.

The claim inverts reality: those unable to afford coverage were exempted, while the only large penalties applied to high earners who chose not to buy insurance. By the 2020 posting date, no federal penalty existed at all.

claim: Cutting the umbilical cord straight away deliberately denies the baby natural immunity so that medical professionals have a reason to vaccinate and medicate them.
justification: Medical evidence shows maternal antibody transfer to the baby occurs via the placenta during pregnancy, not through leaving the umbilical cord attached after birth, and cord-clamping-timing research concerns blood volume/iron stores rather than disease immunity. There is no scientific support for the claim that cord-cutting is a deliberate scheme to strip immunity so professionals can justify vaccination; sterile cord-cutting is in fact a recognized infection-prevention measure.

trace.raw_text:
Based on my research, I could not locate the specific Facebook post by this named individual, but I found substantial scientific evidence directly relevant to the underlying medical claim.

**What the evidence shows:**

Maternal antibodies are transferred to a baby primarily through the placenta *during pregnancy*, not through the umbilical cord after birth. The placenta generally does not allow bacteria to enter the fetal bloodstream, and can even provide a barrier against some viruses, while also transferring some large molecules, like maternal antibodies, to the fetus. This process begins well before delivery: maternal antibodies steadily build in the fetal bloodstream from about 17 weeks on, with a sharp surge in the month before birth.

Delayed cord clamping research focuses on blood volume and iron benefits, not on withholding "immunity." Studies have shown that delayed umbilical cord clamping is associated with a greater haemoglobin concentration in the newborns and best iron storage between 3-6 months of life and less incidence for transfusion and neonatal hypotension. Nothing in the clinical literature frames cord-cutting as a deliberate mechanism to strip away disease immunity so that "medical professionals have a reason to vaccinate."

Separately, cutting the cord with sterile instruments is itself a protective public-health measure against infection, not an act designed to create vulnerability: A newly cut umbilical cord can be a pathway for bacteria that can cause newborn sepsis and death, and optimal umbilical cord care practices has the potential to avoid these preventable neonatal deaths. Historically, *unsanitary* (not sanitary) cord cutting has been the actual danger, as seen with neonatal tetanus in low-resource settings — the opposite of the claim's framing that clean/early cutting is the harmful, profit-motivated act.

**Assessment:** The claim rests on a conspiratorial premise — that cutting the cord deliberately deprives infants of "natural immunity" for commercial/medical gain. Actual immunology shows maternal antibody transfer happens via the placenta before birth, cord-clamping timing studies relate to blood/iron volume (not disease immunity), and sterile cord-cutting is a protective, not harmful, practice. No credible source supports an intentional scheme to deny babies immunity in order to justify vaccination.

In the UK, Public Health England was publishing weekly mortality reports, and researchers used these reports to analyze whether COVID-19 was the underlying cause of death using Public Health England (PHE) weekly reports on excess mortality (published since the week ending 3 July 2020). In the US, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) post weekly data on mortality for 13 causes of death from the most prevalent comorbid conditions reported on death certificates where COVID-19 was listed as a cause of death. Academic analyses using this published data were already determining where COVID-19 ranked among causes of death, finding for example that based on the reported number of COVID-19 deaths, COVID-19 had the second leading number of deaths in the USA, however, since the number of reported deaths could also be under-reported, this means that COVID-19 could have potentially been the leading cause of death in the USA in 2020.

The claim comes from a debate on Oct. 8, 2020, where Miller-Meeks stated this exact line. On the Mann Act: Ginsburg wrote that the Mann Act (which punishes those who engage in interstate sex traffic of women and girls) is "offensive," and that such acts should be considered "within the zone of privacy." Based on my research, I found clear context for evaluating this claim.

**What's confirmed:** Ventura County did dramatically reduce the number of physical in-person voting locations for the November 2020 election. According to local news coverage, there were about 50 polling locations in Ventura County compared to about 400 in previous years, long before the COVID-19 pandemic. This reduction was real and documented.

**What the reduction actually represented:** The change was not an isolated suppression tactic — it was part of California's statewide Voter's Choice Act (VCA) model, which Ventura County had adopted. claim: A US voter can vote 4 times because he got 4 vote by mail forms.
justification: The specific Facebook post by James Snapp could not be located directly, but the claim matches a widely circulated and debunked 2020 narrative. Fact-checkers (AP, PolitiFact) and election security experts confirmed that receiving multiple mail ballot forms does not allow a person to vote multiple times, since signature verification and ballot logging systems prevent double voting, and such an attempt would constitute felony voter fraud.

trace.raw_text:
I could not find the specific James Snapp Facebook post from September 16, 2020, but I found substantial evidence about the underlying factual claim—that receiving multiple vote-by-mail forms would allow someone to vote multiple times. This type of claim circulated widely on Facebook in 2020 and was consistently debunked.

A nearly identical claim—that a couple who received five vote-by-mail applications at their address would be able to send them back and receive five ballots to vote multiple times—was fact-checked by both the Associated Press and PolitiFact and found to be false, with the post later marked by Facebook as containing "False Information" based on two independent fact checks.

Election security experts explained why this doesn't work: "The way it works is, people can no more vote multiple mail ballots than they could go into various different polling places on Election Day and try to vote," said David Becker, founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research. Additionally, when election officials mail out a ballot to a voter, they verify that the voter's signature on the ballot application form matches the voter's signature on file. Receiving multiple blank *applications* for a mail ballot (often due to administrative overlap between state mailings and outside groups) does not result in multiple actual ballots being issued or counted — only one ballot per registered voter is processed, and whoever engages in such behavior as described would also be committing a felony, as voter fraud is a criminal offense punishable by up to five years in prison.

More broadly, comprehensive post-election analysis found essentially no evidence of this type of fraud occurring at scale: a new reporting project from the Associated Press shows that is false, finding fewer than 475 potential instances out of more than 25 million votes cast. State-level guardrails, such as Pennsylvania's, confirm in no event may a voter cast more than one ballot, and safeguards in the Pennsylvania system will prevent them from doing so.

While I cannot verify the exact wording or context of James Snapp's specific Facebook post, the general claim he is reported to have made — that a voter could cast multiple ballots simply because they received multiple vote-by-mail forms — matches a well-documented category of 2020 misinformation that was repeatedly and specifically debunked by election officials and fact-checkers.

claim: The rate of abortions under Democratic presidential administrations has actually fallen more precipitously.
justification: CDC and Guttmacher data do show steeper abortion rate declines during the Clinton and Obama administrations compared to Republican administrations since the 1980s, which supports the literal claim. However, this omits that the Democratic Carter administration saw a sharp increase, that CDC data changes (California dropping out) exaggerate the Clinton-era drop, and that fact-checkers like Snopes and PolitiFact conclude there is little evidence of a real correlation between presidential party and abortion rates once causation and state-level policy are considered.

trace.raw_text:
## Fact-Check Summary

The claim—that abortion rates have fallen more steeply under Democratic presidential administrations than Republican ones—is a numerically accurate but context-stripped statement that multiple sources, including fact-checkers and even pro-life advocacy groups, have scrutinized.

**What the data shows:** Using CDC data, during the last three decades, abortion rates have fallen the most under Democrats, and remained flat or at best decreased marginally under Republican administrations. Specifically, under Bill Clinton (1993-2001), abortion rates fell from 23 to 16.2 per every 1,000 women, while George W. Bush saw rates hover around 16 before dropping slightly, and then rates plunged from 15 per 1,000 women in 2009 to 11.6 in 2016 under Obama.

Even sources skeptical of the political framing concede the underlying numbers: it is true that there were larger abortion rate declines during the presidential administrations of Democrats Bill Clinton and Barack Obama than the administrations of Ronald Reagan, George H.W. Bush, and George W. Bush.

**Important context that complicates the claim:**

1. **Carter exception:** Critics note that proponents of this claim nearly all neglect to mention that the U.S. abortion rate rose sharply during the presidential administration of Democrat Jimmy Carter, undermining the idea that *all* Democratic administrations see steeper declines.

2. **Data reliability issues:** Some memes use CDC abortion data, and the fact that California stopped reporting its abortion data to the CDC in 1997 explains why some memes report a very large decline in abortion numbers during the Clinton administration.

3. **Causation vs. correlation:** Snopes' analysis, cited by several sources, concludes that abortion rates have risen and fallen under both Democratic and Republican administrations, suggesting little to no correlation with whichever political party controls the White House, with the overall trend since the 1980s being a fairly consistent decline across administrations of both parties. Snopes further notes one can argue that the rate of decline appeared to slow during the presidency of George W. Bush before increasing under President Barack Obama's administration, but such an observation would be based on a comparison between only two administrations and would do nothing to demonstrate causation.

4. **Experts caution against oversimplification:** A PolitiFact analysis found that what happens at the state level really affects abortion rates, and experts said tying the abortion rate to the occupant of the White House alone is an oversimplification of a variety of factors that are at play.

**Bottom line:** The raw statistical comparison (Clinton/Obama vs. Reagan/Bush eras showing steeper declines) is factually supported by CDC and Guttmacher data. However, the claim omits that this pattern doesn't hold for all Democratic presidents (Carter), that data-reporting changes (California's exit from CDC reporting) inflate the apparent Clinton-era drop, and that experts broadly reject any causal link between presidential party and abortion rates—making the claim's implied takeaway misleading even though its core numerical comparison is accurate.

The JCPOA (2015 nuclear deal), which took effect on "Implementation Day" in January 2016, required Iran to not exceed 300 kilograms (kg) of UF6 containing 3.67% u-235 "or the equivalent in other chemical forms." This 300 kg limit reflected the drastically reduced stockpile Iran held as of early 2016, after it shipped out the vast majority of its previously accumulated enriched uranium to comply with the deal.

By September 2020, just before Biden made this claim, the IAEA said that Iran's stockpile of low-enriched uranium reached 2,105 kilograms, or about 10 times more than the JCPOA limit. This was corroborated by an independent nuclear analysis organization, which found that Iran's low enriched uranium (LEU) stock now exceeds by ten-fold the limit set in the JCPOA, with a stockpile of about 3114.5 kilograms of LEU (hexafluoride mass), equivalent to 2105.4 kg (uranium mass) as of Aug 25, 2020.

Since the JCPOA's 300 kg cap was essentially the stockpile level Iran was held to beginning in 2016, describing the September 2020 stockpile as "10 times as much as it had in 2016" is functionally equivalent to the IAEA's own framing of "10 times the JCPOA limit." The Wikipedia summary of Iran's nuclear program timeline likewise notes that in September 2020, the IAEA reported that Iran had accumulated ten times as much enriched uranium as permitted by the JCPOA, confirming the figure was being widely reported at the time Biden made this statement.

But Trump's framing — that this was Biden personally 'managing' swine flu and doing everything wrong — omits that Klain wasn't involved in the H1N1 response and was speaking about the administration generally, that Klain later clarified the remark referred specifically to vaccine-production difficulties, and that independent assessments rated the actual 2009 response as largely effective.

trace.raw_text:
The core quote attributed to Trump is factually accurate but presented with misleading context. Ron Klain, who later became Biden's chief of staff, did say in a May 2019 speech at a biosecurity summit: "We did every possible thing wrong — 60 million Americans got H1N1," he said at a biosecurity summit in May 2019. He added: "It had nothing to do with us doing anything right. It just had to do with luck."

However, several important contextual facts complicate the claim as framed by Trump:

1. **Klain wasn't describing Biden's personal management of the response.** Ron Klain, Biden's former chief of staff, has criticized the Obama administration's swine flu response, not Biden specifically. In fact, Klain did not head up the response to the H1N1 virus, he was working for Biden at the time. He was, however, the administration's Ebola czar.

2. **Klain later clarified the specific meaning of his remark.** Klain later told Politico his comments referred to the administration's difficulties producing enough of the vaccine they developed, and argued the Obama team quickly adapted to the pandemic — quickly responding and distributing supplies from the federal stockpile, for example — and made very different choices than the Trump administration.

3. **Independent assessments of the actual swine flu response were largely positive**, contradicting the sweeping "did everything wrong" framing Trump used. The swine flu is estimated to have killed 12,000 people in the U.S., far fewer than the more than 200,000 who have died of Covid-19 to date. The Obama administration also got generally high marks for its response to the swine flu. While government reports after the fact identified room for growth, they also highlighted successes, like rapid research and development of a vaccine that arrived in less than six months.

So while Trump accurately quotes a real Klain statement, he uses it to imply Biden personally mismanaged the entire swine flu response — an impression Klain himself later disavowed, and one not supported by the broader record of the 2009 response, which experts generally rated positively.

I have sufficient evidence to evaluate this claim.

This refers to the viral September 2020 video (by retired anesthesiologist Dr. Ted Noel, though the question attributes it to "Étienne Lolkek" on YouTube) showing vape smoke escaping through various face masks, which was widely circulated as "proof" masks don't work against COVID-19.

Multiple public health experts and fact-checkers examined this video and rejected its conclusion. A YouTube video and social media posts claim a man blowing vape smoke through various face masks shows that they do not help prevent the spread of coronavirus. This is false; experts agree that while the virus itself is small enough to fit through mask fibers -- as is vape smoke -- masks do help. Dr. John O'Horo, an infectious disease specialist at Mayo Clinic, noted that "The idea that just seeing some particulates going through a mask negates their effectiveness is just a misunderstanding of how masks work." He further explained that the masks do allow air and small particles to pass through, that's how we can still breathe with them on, but what they do is they take a lot of the energy out so it doesn't travel as far.

Epidemiologist Cindy Prins called the video "completely misleading," saying "Fabric and surgical/procedure masks are meant to help protect against larger droplet particles that may contain COVID-19." Dr. Shelley Payne noted that masks also help prevent aerosol transmission, and much of the leakage of aerosols shown in the video is at the edges of the mask, with less from the front, reducing exposure to a person you are facing and talking to.

Additional scientific analysis found that vape smoke introduces billions more particles in a single saturated breath than would be exhaled during normal breathing, talking, or even a cough, making the demonstration show far more particles than realistic exposure. An academic review of such e-cigarette demonstrations likewise noted there is no empiric evidence of aerial transmission of the SARS-CoV-2 virus through environmental e-cigarette aerosol exhaled by infected vapers.

**On the case counts:** By the date this claim was made (September 3, 2020), reporting already showed case numbers far exceeding "88." More than two weeks after nearly half a million bikers flocked to South Dakota, the tally of coronavirus infections traced back to the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally had surpassed 260, an estimate that was growing steadily as more states reported cases and at least one death. Even just within South Dakota, "Currently 40 cases have been reported to the South Dakota Department of Health related to the Sturgis Rally," including "three out-of-state cases that we were notified of because those cases had close contact with a South Dakota resident." By early September, the Associated Press had projected 124 in-state cases tied to Sturgis, and 290 across multiple states. A CDC-led investigation later found the 2020 event had "many characteristics of a superspreading event," resulting in 463 primary cases reported within two weeks of the rally and another 186 identified as secondary contacts, for a total of 649 cases traced to the event.

**On the "no more cases than rest of state" assertion:** This is directly contradicted by state-level data. South Dakota's own positivity rate was climbing during this period: on Aug. 7, the opening day of the rally, South Dakota had roughly 9,000 COVID-19 cases; by Aug. 26, positive cases had risen to 11,500, and the state's positivity rate also rose, from 6% for the 14 days before Aug. 7, to 9% for the 14 days before Aug. 26. Based on the fact-check findings, there is no official statistical body in Nigeria—including the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS)—that tracks GDP or income data by ethnicity. The NBS spokesperson explicitly stated that the claim is "not statistically correct" as there is no basis for the assertion. This is because the NBS does not compute GDP on the basis of ethnic nationalities and the National Population Commission did not collect data analysed based on ethnicity in the last census held in 2006, meaning the population of Igbo people remains unknown.

At the continental level, standard GDP-per-capita rankings also contradict the notion that any Nigerian ethnic group could plausibly top Africa, since Nigeria itself ranks far below smaller, wealthier economies—countries like Seychelles, Africa's richest country per capita in 2026, with Mauritius ranking second and Gabon third—while Nigeria's output is divided across more than 220 million people, giving it a GDP per capita of roughly $1,100–$1,300, placing it in the bottom half of African countries per person.

Legal sources confirm that sex offender registration exemptions ('Romeo and Juliet' provisions) require both a small age gap (typically 2-4 years) and an older minor victim (usually 13+), and that offenses against children under 13-14 (like what a 21-year-old having sex with an 11-year-old would constitute) trigger mandatory registration in virtually every US jurisdiction. This claim closely matches the controversy surrounding California's SB 145, authored by State Sen. Scott Wiener, which became law in September 2020. The claim appears to be a version of the misleading framing that critics like Donald Trump Jr. and Ted Cruz used against the bill. The actual facts are important here: a bill signed into California law in September 2020 gives judges discretion over whether to require someone convicted of statutory rape to register as a sex offender, but did not alter any existing penalties for sexual assault, rape, or child exploitation. Critics characterized it as enabling child abuse, but this mischaracterized what the law actually does.

Crucially, SB 145's judicial discretion provision applies specifically to close-in-age "Romeo and Juliet" style statutory rape cases (minors and young adults close in age, with voluntary sexual activity), not to adults committing child molestation against pre-pubescent children like an 11-year-old. A 21-year-old having sex with an 11-year-old would constitute an entirely different and far more serious category of crime (child molestation/lewd acts with a child under 14, aggravated sexual assault of a child, etc.) in every US state, and such offenses carry mandatory sex offender registration — this is confirmed by legal references showing that offenses like lewd acts with a minor under 14 require registration, and that age-gap exceptions in registration laws (Romeo and Juliet provisions) require the parties to be close in age (typically within 2-4 years) and the victim to be an older minor (generally 13+), not an 11-year-old paired with a 21-year-old. There is no state law exemption that would let a 21-year-old who sexually abuses an 11-year-old avoid the sex offender registry.

This claim represents a distorted exaggeration of the actual, narrower effect of laws like SB 145 — it takes a real controversy about judicial discretion for close-in-age offenders and misapplies it to an extreme, unrelated scenario (a 10-year age gap with a prepubescent child) that no such law covers.

claim: Face masks cause hypoxia.
justification: Multiple fact-checks, medical experts, and a controlled peer-reviewed study (50 subjects) found zero cases of hypoxemia from wearing cloth or surgical masks at rest or during exercise. This claim—that face masks cause hypoxia—has been extensively fact-checked and found to be false for the general healthy population. Multiple medical experts and peer-reviewed research consistently show that normal face masks (cloth, surgical) do not reduce blood oxygen levels in healthy individuals.

A peer-reviewed study testing 50 adults found that facemasks did not impair oxygenation or ventilation among 50 adults at rest or during physical activity, with no episodes of hypoxemia or hypercarbia occurring with either cloth or surgical masks, both at rest and while walking briskly, and the risk of pathologic gas exchange impairment with cloth masks and surgical masks is near-zero in the general adult population.

Medical experts have directly addressed this claim. A pulmonary specialist stated there's "no evidence that wearing a mask impairs oxygen delivery or carbon dioxide elimination from the body." Similarly, an emergency medicine director noted "As far as hypoxia goes, there's little to no data that shows that's true." Physics also makes the claim implausible, as one doctor explained: "The size of an oxygen molecule is so small that there's no way that a mask could restrict the movement of oxygen"

The only caveat experts raise is for people with pre-existing severe respiratory conditions: research articles and experts suggest that such symptoms are unlikely to occur in most people, unless the wearer has pre-existing respiratory illnesses such as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and even then the effects are minor rather than true hypoxia in most cases. One study specific to severe asthma patients found that while a KF-94 mask slightly lowered oxygen saturation after exercise, although wearing the KF-94 mask statistically lowered the saturation after 6MWT, it was still within the normal physiologic range.

The general claim, as stated broadly (face masks cause hypoxia), misrepresents the scientific consensus, which is that normal mask use does not cause hypoxia in the general population.

That investigation further noted after the project fizzled out in 2004, the regulators approved Fox for broadcast on Canadian airwaves via satellite in the same year. So right now, Canadians can watch Bill O'Reilly, Megyn Kelly, Fox & Friends and everyone else through several private dish providers. No reporting from mainstream outlets, the Department of Energy, or the White House itself supports the sweeping takeover described in the Facebook claim.

trace.raw_text:
Based on my research, I found no evidence supporting the specific claim as stated. The actual executive order Trump signed around that time (Executive Order 13920, signed May 1, 2020) was narrowly scoped: President Trump issued an executive order declaring a national emergency over threats to the U.S. power system, and the order bans the use of equipment for the power grid that was manufactured by a company under the control of a foreign adversary, or the buying of any equipment that poses a national security threat.

The order specifically defined its scope narrowly: The Order defines "bulk-power system" to mean facilities and control systems necessary for operating an interconnected electric energy transmission network, including transmission lines rated at 69,000 volts (69 kV) or more, while facilities used in the local distribution of electricity are excluded.

This is fundamentally different from the Facebook claim, which asserts a sweeping "White House takeover" of "all electrical grids" that would encompass "internet servers, broadcasting systems and electronic systems." The real order:

1. Did not "take over" the power grid — it restricted foreign-sourced equipment and established review/procurement procedures, with the Energy Secretary (not "the White House" directly) given authority over specific equipment decisions.
2. Did not cover the entire electrical grid — it explicitly excluded local distribution systems.
3. Said nothing about internet servers or broadcasting systems — these were not mentioned in the order, which was strictly about bulk-power system hardware.

No independent fact-checking source or news outlet from 2020 corroborates the broader "takeover of internet, broadcasting, and electronic systems" framing; this appears to be a significant distortion/exaggeration of the actual, narrower cybersecurity-focused order.

claim: The Edo State government of Nigeria receives 600 million naira monthly as a security vote.
justification: Ize-Iyamu did repeatedly make this exact claim during the 2020 campaign, as confirmed by multiple contemporaneous news reports quoting him directly. However, Nigerian 'security votes' are notoriously undisclosed and not itemized in public budgets, and the N600 million figure was explicitly presented as his campaign's own estimate/calculation rather than an official or independently verified figure; other sources from the same period cite different estimates (e.g., roughly $2 million monthly), making the precise monthly amount impossible to independently confirm.

Based on my research, this claim traces back to statements Pastor Osagie Ize-Iyamu made during the September 2020 Edo governorship campaign, when he was the APC candidate challenging incumbent Governor Godwin Obaseki.

**What the record shows:**

Ize-Iyamu did make this exact claim repeatedly. In an interview on ARISE News during the campaign, he stated: "you can't be collecting over N600 million monthly and what we have been able to calculate that you spend maximum is N20 million. How can you spend only 20 million on security when you collected 600 million, what are you doing with the balance." He repeated the figure again: "From our calculations, you can't be collecting 600 million monthly, only spending about 20 million."

He also tied this to an annual figure, saying "When this governor came in, the security vote was around 4.5 billion annually. He came in and increased it to 7.5 billion, which is like almost 100 percent increase" — a figure that, divided by 12, roughly aligns with his ~600 million monthly claim.

**However, this figure is not independently verifiable:**

Security votes in Nigeria are notoriously opaque. As one analysis noted, "Based on the sensitive nature of intelligence gathering for security purposes, the said monies cannot be accounted for." Estimates of Edo's security vote vary across sources: one opinion piece referenced a "$2million monthly security vote," while a Wikipedia compilation (reflecting a different, more recent period) lists Edo State: N900M Monthly (N10.8B Annually). Official Edo State budget documents I found broke out a separate "Security Trust Fund" line (N2 billion annually) but did not publicly itemize a specific "security vote" figure, which is consistent with how these funds are typically handled off public budget books nationwide.

So while Ize-Iyamu certainly made this exact claim, it was explicitly presented as his campaign's own calculation/estimate ("what we have been able to calculate") rather than a disclosed official figure, and no independent/official source confirms the precise N600 million monthly amount for that period.

This was from his RNC acceptance speech on the South Lawn of the White House.

However, PBS NewsHour's fact-check of this exact statement found it quite misleading, noting that those orders haven't taken effect yet — the text of one hasn't even been made publicly available — and experts told us that, if implemented, the measures would be unlikely to result in significant drug price reductions for the majority of Americans.

The White House's own materials described the orders as designed to massively lower prescription drug costs and increase Americans' access to life-saving medications, including insulin, but this was the administration's characterization of its own policy, not an independent verification of actual price reductions.

justification: Ernst did make this statement verbatim at the 2020 RNC, but its central assertion—that Biden/Democrats would 'essentially ban animal agriculture and eliminate gas-powered cars'—is false. PolitiFact rated the claim False, noting Biden never endorsed the Green New Deal resolution, which itself does not call for ending animal agriculture or gas-powered cars, and a Stanford climate scientist called the causal link 'unfounded.' This claim has been directly fact-checked by multiple outlets with consistent conclusions.

Joni Ernst did make this statement verbatim at the 2020 RNC: "The Democratic Party of Joe Biden is pushing this so-called Green New Deal. If given power, they would essentially ban animal agriculture and eliminate gas-powered cars."

However, fact-checkers found the substance of the claim to be false. PolitiFact Iowa examined the claim and concluded: Ernst's and Trump's claims that Biden would eliminate animal agriculture and gas powered cars if elected president aren't true because Biden has never endorsed the Green New Deal legislation as written, and while Biden agrees with some basic principles of the legislation, the resolution would not eliminate animal agriculture or gas-powered cars. The ruling was False.

Regarding Biden's actual position, his Iowa campaign spokeswoman stated Biden never endorsed the Green New Deal resolution. The Green New Deal resolution itself, examined by The Hill, calls for supporting family farming and building a more sustainable food system, but does not call for the end of animal agriculture; similarly, it calls for investing in zero-emission vehicle infrastructure but does not endorse getting rid of gas-powered vehicles.

A Stanford earth systems science professor who studied the Green New Deal added that the claim that eliminating greenhouse emissions would lead to the elimination of animal agriculture is unfounded. Biden's own climate plan, separate from the Green New Deal resolution, does not call for an end to gasoline cars, but he does hope to tighten emissions standards and speed up the use of electric vehicles. Similarly, his agriculture plan calls for decarbonizing the food and agriculture sector but doesn't say it will get rid of livestock.

A nearly identical claim by Trump that the Green New Deal would "ban cows" was also separately rated False by PolitiFact, which noted there is no actual mention of cows in the deal's text.

claim: Joe Biden is for open borders, sanctuary cities, free lawyers and health care for illegal immigrants.
justification: Contemporaneous fact-checks (NPR and others) of this exact RNC speech found that Biden did not support 'open borders,' did not promise 'free lawyers' (his plan added asylum officers/interpreters, not free legal counsel), and did not propose taxpayer-subsidized 'free health care' for illegal immigrants (only emergency care already mandated by law, or an unsubsidized public-option buy-in). Only the 'sanctuary cities' portion accurately reflects Biden's stated 2020 position of limiting local-federal immigration enforcement cooperation.

Based on the NPR/contemporaneous fact-check of this exact speech, Pence's claim is a compound statement that mischaracterizes several of Biden's actual 2020 positions.

**On "open borders":** NPR's fact-check found on "open borders," Biden does not support "open borders," but he would undo many of the Trump Administration's policies designed to restrict immigration. His actual plan supports accepting more refugees into the country, setting the cap at 125,000 annually, up from the current cap of 18,000, and calls for bolstering border security.

**On "free lawyers":** Fact-checkers found Biden's plan calls for adding asylum officers, immigration judges, court staff and interpreters, but does not promise free lawyers.

**On "free health care":** Biden has said people who came to the country illegally should have access to emergency care, which is already mandated by federal law. Under Biden's health care plan, he has said they could buy into a public option, but it would not be subsidized by the taxpayer.

**On "sanctuary cities":** This is the most accurate part of the claim — in a plan outlining his agenda for the Latino community, the campaign says Biden would "limit" the use programs that force local law enforcement to assist federal immigration authorities in immigration enforcement. Separate reporting confirms he promised to protect sanctuary cities from federal law enforcement agencies.

Overall, NPR explicitly labeled this line among several inaccurate or questionable claims Pence deployed in the speech. Three of the four elements (open borders, free lawyers, free health care) are mischaracterizations or overstatements of Biden's actual stated positions, while only the "sanctuary cities" portion is reasonably accurate.

justification: Trump did say this exact line in his Aug 27, 2020 RNC speech, but independent fact-checks (Roll Call/FactCheck.org, Breaking Defense/CSIS experts) found the $2.5 trillion figure misleading: it represents total DoD budget outlays (actually ~$2.9 trillion inflation-adjusted for 2017-2020), not spending specifically on 'rebuilding' equipment, which made up only about 20% of that total and was actually lower as a share than under Obama. The claim that the military was 'completely rebuilt' with this spending and was previously 'very badly depleted' is not supported by the budget breakdown.

trace.raw_text:
Trump did make this exact statement during his RNC acceptance speech on August 27, 2020, as confirmed by the transcript. However, fact-checkers found the $2.5 trillion figure itself to be inaccurate.

According to Roll Call's fact-check of the speech, the president falsely claimed that his administration had spent nearly $2.5 trillion on completely rebuilding the military, which was very badly depleted when he took office. The actual figures don't match this framing: Trump's $2.5 trillion figure roughly refers to the total amount of Defense Department budgets from 2017 to 2020, which actually totaled $2.9 trillion in inflation-adjusted dollars. More importantly, the claim conflates total defense budget with equipment spending specifically—procurement of new equipment made up only 20.3 percent of those 2017-2020 defense budgets, or $590.7 billion, which was actually 5.8 percent lower than the 2009-2012 budgets under Obama's first term.

A separate Breaking Defense analysis of an earlier, similar claim by Trump found that Trump definitely drove a sharp buildup in defense spending after years of cuts under Obama, but today's spending levels were hardly unprecedented, with both George W. Bush and Obama spending more each year from 2007 through 2012 when adjusted for inflation. Additionally, his claim to have outspent previous administrations is not true, since comparing inflation-adjusted dollars, the government spent more on defense every year from 2007 through 2012.

The claim also implies the military was being "rebuilt" from depletion, but experts note procurement/modernization spending—the part most associated with "rebuilding"—was actually lower as a share of the budget than under Obama, undercutting the "badly depleted" framing. A more recent analysis similarly notes that the increase under Trump was often highlighted in his speeches where he claimed to have invested $2.5 trillion in military equipment, but only 20% of that budget was actually spent on purchasing new equipment.

claim: It's NOT a SECOND WAVE of COVID-19 coming soon. It's the NORMAL COLD / FLU SEASON
justification: The claim conflates COVID-19 with ordinary seasonal cold/flu illness, but COVID-19 is a distinct, more severe disease, and historical data show the 2020-2021 flu season was abnormally mild (not 'normal') due to COVID mitigation measures, while COVID-19 itself caused a massive, well-documented surge in cases and deaths that fall/winter that was tracked separately from flu surveillance.

trace.raw_text:
Based on my research, this claim can be assessed as follows:

The claim, made in September 2020, suggested that an anticipated rise in illness that fall would just be "normal cold/flu season" rather than a genuine COVID-19 resurgence — implying COVID concerns were being overblown or conflated with ordinary seasonal illness.

This framing is contradicted by the actual historical record. First, COVID-19 is a distinct, novel coronavirus with a far greater fatality rate compared with the flu, along with a much higher rate of hospitalisations and severe infection, making it fundamentally different from ordinary cold/flu illness, not a disguised version of it.

Second, what actually happened in fall/winter 2020 directly contradicts the "normal flu season" framing. Contemporary CDC/WHO data showed the opposite of a normal flu season — health authorities observed lower than usual flu activity in October 2020, which is generally the month in which flu season begins, largely because the widespread adoption of public health measures to reduce the spread of COVID-19, such as wearing masks and physical distancing, likely contributed, in part, to the lower flu activity observed. Meanwhile, COVID-19 itself went on to cause a massive, well-documented surge in cases, hospitalizations, and deaths in the following months (the actual "second wave" in the U.S.), which was tracked and attributed specifically to COVID-19, not ordinary seasonal flu/cold illness.

So rather than the fall 2020 uptick being "just normal cold/flu season," flu activity was abnormally suppressed that year while COVID-19 surged as a distinct, more severe disease — the opposite of what the claim asserts.
